A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DAG-Math work. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and the retained equations, experiments, tables and figures can be matched reliably.

before.justification: V1 reports original benchmark construction, graph statistics and evaluations of five LLMs on AIME 2025, BRUMO 2025 and HMMT 2025, including additional results in Appendix F.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds human validation, larger-sample estimates, prompt and parser comparisons, cross-family demonstrations and thinking-mode experiments.

M1.justification: The core DAG model, stochastic sampling rule and PRR definitions remain unchanged. Sections H and K.3 add a post-hoc dependency-parsing procedure for natural CoT, with separate prompts for thinking models and reason-then-dependency annotation for non-thinking models. This extends the evaluation procedure beyond directly generated DAG-MATH outputs.

E1.justification: The original Omni-MATH construction data and three evaluation datasets remain. Appendix B.2 adds a single IMO 2025 Q4 proof case using a lemma-level DAG drawn from Claude-Opus-4-6. This extends case-study coverage to an IMO proof without establishing a broader IMO benchmark evaluation.

E2.justification: The original five-model comparison is retained. The added GPT-4.1/AIME study compares natural CoT against DAG-MATH and adds external parsing by GPT-o4-mini and Gemini-2.5-Flash-Thinking against self-parsing (Table 11). These comparator additions are confined to the supplementary validation studies.

E3.justification: V2 adds several evaluation designs: a random 50-problem human/SymPy audit, prompt perturbations, external reparsing, zero-shot natural CoT versus four-shot DAG-MATH, matched demonstration problems generated by different model families, and thinking-on/off controls. The original evaluation remains reported. The natural-CoT comparison changes both formatting and demonstration count, so it does not isolate formatting alone.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's graph-statistics analyses and heptagon case study, v2 investigates benchmark dependency correctness, prompt sensitivity, parser consistency and circularity, formatting constraints, demonstration-family bias and thinking modes. Appendices E and K provide substantial new validation and robustness analyses; Appendix B.2 adds the IMO proof case.

E5.justification: V1 reports 32 trajectories per problem and cross-model standard deviations. V2 explicitly increases sampling to 128 trajectories for four models on AIME, adds Wilson 95% confidence intervals for PASS@1-minus-PRR gaps, and introduces TOST equivalence testing with 90% intervals, p-values and stated margins. These are substantial additions to statistical reporting.

E6.justification: The original numerical tables are retained as v2 Tables 1 and 4–6. New results include 49/50 audit samples passing dependency checks, larger-sample estimates in Table 7, Gemini Flash thinking-mode PASS@1/PRR of 64.0%/35.9%, and prompt, parser and demonstration-family comparisons. These are additional experimental results, not improvements under the unchanged original settings. Figure 10's family labels conflict with Table 12.

T1.justification: The main definitions and mathematical framework remain unchanged. Appendix A.3 adds an argument connecting finite proof dependencies to acyclicity, including proof by contradiction. Appendix B.2 adds a worked number-theoretic characterization and sufficiency/necessity proof sketch for IMO 2025 Q4, rather than a new general theorem about DAG-Math.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution statements and conclusion retain the same central claims: the DAG stochastic framework, logical closeness and PRR, the 2,894-graph benchmark, and the distinction between answer accuracy and reasoning fidelity. The additional studies do not redefine these headline contributions.

C2.justification: Sections 5.1 and K add substantive interpretations that logical closeness is intrinsic rather than parser-induced, structured formatting encourages coherence, cross-family demonstrations preserve conclusions, and thinking improves exploration without eliminating the reasoning gap. Appendix A.3 broadens the applicability discussion to theorem proving, while Appendix J proposes specific search-reward and RL-curriculum uses.

D1.justification: V2 supplies full sensitivity and parsing prompts, a human-validation pipeline with a SymPy example, validator identities, retry/filtering rules, and the AUC threshold increment. Appendix D names GPT-4o and GPT-o3 validation roles. The advertised repository address also changes. These expanded disclosures do not establish that the original benchmark was regenerated.

R1.justification: The main positioning against earlier graph, Markov-chain and tree-based accounts remains. V2 adds the IMO Foundation reference and discusses potential connections to Monte Carlo Tree Search and Tree-of-Thoughts in Appendix J, although those discussion citations appear as unresolved question marks.

P1.justification: Most existing prose, including the introduction and conclusion, is retained. V2 changes the title and affiliation text, revises the acyclicity discussion, adds a Section 5.1 overview, subdivides Appendix B and reorganizes appendices around the additions. This is limited editing and restructuring rather than extensive rewriting of the existing narrative.

P2.justification: V2 substantially expands the visual presentation with the IMO DAG, three new ablation figures, eight additional numbered tables and a displayed SymPy validation example. Existing figures and tables are largely retained but relocated or resized, including the heptagon DAG and supplementary graph-statistics tables. Institutional logos are added to the first page.

improvement.justification: The human/SymPy audit, uncertainty estimates and sensitivity studies provide useful validation missing from v1, with substantially better documentation. However, claims of parser independence exceed the stable-AUC evidence: DAG-MATH PRR varies from 16.8% to 11.4% across parsers in Table 11. New inconsistencies also limit the gain: Table 3 totals 2,879 successes against the stated 2,894 graphs, and Figure 10's family labels conflict with Table 12. The added evidence supports a limited net improvement.
